summary: SoK of secure code generation plus a three-layer measurement framework (KAUGE): a 6,382-question NL benchmark of OWASP/CERT secure-coding principles (knowledge), executable CWEval and BaxBench runs (actuation), and an LLM-judged exploit-to-principle compliance check (gap). Finds models score 86-97% on principle knowledge but far lower on functional-and-secure code, and that a Codex agent scaffold gives the largest actuation gains.

claims.claim: Secure-coding-principle understanding is a statistically strong predictor of code-level outcomes.
claims.evidence: §V/Appendix C: across 10 base models Spearman rho=0.71, p=0.025 for CWEval secure-pass@k and rho=0.63, p=0.056 (not significant) for BaxBench. The n=18 rho=0.75 in §VI pools method slices that share the same per-model K value, so the slices are not independent. 'Statistically strong' in the abstract overstates a borderline n=10 result.

claims.claim: Large knowledge-actuation gaps persist: models know principles but fail to produce secure functional code.
claims.evidence: Fig. 1: Layer-1 scores 86.2-97%; Table III: secure-pass@1 3.8-91.6; reported gap 47.9 points (CWEval) and 72.9 (BaxBench); Wilcoxon n=18 p<.001. The direction is robust, but K (fixed-answer NLU accuracy) and A (secure-pass@1) are on incommensurable scales, so the gap's magnitude has no clear meaning.

claims.claim: Agentic scaffolding (Codex) improves actuation most, by improving software construction rather than security knowledge.
claims.evidence: Table III: GPT-5.1-Codex-Mini base vs Codex Scaffold secure-pass@1 60.5->91.6 (CWEval), 34.2->41.8 (BaxBench). This is one sample per task with no repeats; the causal attribution to 'construction' is interpretive.

claims.claim: Inference-time interventions (security prompting, RCI) steer rather than add capability; RCI breaks functionality.
claims.evidence: Table III: RCI pass@1 drops 68.9->48.7 (Qwen) and 84.9->59.7 (GPT); paired tests: Security-Aware prompt on GPT 20 vs 6 security flips p=0.009, functionality p=0.607.

claims.claim: Security fine-tuning/RL (SafeCoder, PurpCodeRL) does not reliably improve joint functional-security correctness.
claims.evidence: Table III: PurpCodeRL secure-pass@1 30.3 vs base 41.2 (CWEval), 4.6 vs 3.8 (BaxBench); SafeCoder better only on BaxBench (8.4). Only Qwen2.5-14B backbone.

patterns.note: Recommends executable exploit/functional feedback over security intent (§VII-A); the agent scaffold with shell/tests gives the largest gains (Table III).

The two-LLM compliance judge gets 82.3% reweighted accuracy against one human annotator, and the two judges have kappa=0.588 with each other; the authors treat its verdicts as diagnostic, not ground truth.
Deliberately avoids static-analysis oracles because of FP/FN; argues clean SAST verdicts can mask exploitable flaws.
Security RL post-training (PurpCodeRL) reduced joint functional-secure pass on both benchmarks.
File-system and shell-capable Codex scaffold outperforms prompt-only generation on both benchmarks.

methodology.sample: CWEval 119 tasks (5 langs, 31 CWEs); BaxBench 392 scenario-framework tasks (6 langs, 13 CWEs); 6,382 NLU questions from 456 rules; 176+ exploit mappings; human validation n=100 per artifact.
methodology.baselines: Base prompt, Security-Aware prompt, RCI, SafeCoder, PurpCodeRL, Codex scaffold: published methods, reasonably current.
methodology.models: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (plus fine-tunes) and GPT-5.1-Codex-Mini in main text; 10 base models for the Appendix C correlation; GPT-5-nano and Claude Haiku 4.5 as judges.
methodology.variance: One sample per task (§V); no seeds or repeats. Paired significance tests and Wilson CIs for human validation only.
methodology.ablations: Interventions act as ablations over a fixed backbone; no ablation of the judge design beyond single-vs-consensus comparison.
methodology.contamination_controls: None; Threats §VIII acknowledges that models may have seen benchmark tasks.
methodology.languages: C, C++, Go, JavaScript, Python (CWEval); Go, JS, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust (BaxBench); no Java.

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/rupampatir/SoK_KAUGE; benchmark on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.20820512).

biases.detail: Abstract calls knowledge a 'statistically strong predictor'; the body shows rho=0.71 p=0.025 (CWEval) and p=0.056 (BaxBench) at n=10.
One generation per task per configuration; no repeated runs despite LLM nondeterminism.
The Layer-3 compliance judge is validated against a single human annotator on n=100; inter-judge kappa 0.588 and 54% of units needed adjudication.
The 'gap' subtracts fixed-answer NLU accuracy from secure-pass@1; the difference between these scales is not a meaningful quantity, and the n=18 correlation pseudo-replicates K across method slices.
Main-text training/inference comparisons use only two backbones (one open, one proprietary).
No controls; CWEval/BaxBench and OWASP/CERT text are public.

coi.affiliations: University at Buffalo, SUNY (all four authors).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GPT-5.1-Codex-Mini / Codex scaffold (OpenAI) evaluated, no vendor authorship.
coi.funding: No acknowledgments/funding section in extracted text.
coi.detail: Academic; the authors' own framework is evaluated with their own judge, but no product is promoted.

verdict_reason: Useful, well-artefacted diagnosis that executable feedback and agent scaffolding beat security prompting and security fine-tuning. However, the headline 'strong predictor' is borderline in the body, there is one sample per task with no variance, the judge is validated against a single annotator, and there is no Java.
applicability: For a Java backend team, the transferable lesson is to not rely on 'be secure' prompt rules or principle text in AGENTS.md files. Put security into executable checks in the verifier loop instead: exploit/negative tests for injection, path traversal, authz and log injection on the ingestion and delivery APIs, run per repo in CI across the several repositories. RCI-style self-critique can break the functional contract (the CBC-to-GCM example), so specs should state security requirements as acceptance tests, not prose. Neither benchmark includes Java, so magnitudes do not transfer directly. Healthcare/PII handling (CWE-522, CWE-117 log injection) is among the recurring failure classes.
